  "text": "The repair shop called on Thursday to say the clock was ready.

“I didn’t leave a clock,” Helen said.

“It’s under your number.”

She looked at the calendar, still turned to August.

“Is it blue?”

“Yes. Kitchen clock.”

Her mother had taken it in before the operation.

At the shop, a man brought it from a shelf behind the counter. He had wrapped the hands in tissue, though the glass protected them.

“New movement,” he said. “Should be fine now.”

“How much?”

“Already paid.”

Helen opened her bag anyway.

“She was particular about the tick,” he said. “Some people want them silent. She didn’t.”

“No.”

He fitted a battery and held the clock towards her. The second hand moved with a small, dry sound.

“Like that?”

“I think so.”

At home, the hook above the kitchen door was hidden by a supermarket calendar. Helen took the calendar down. A pale circle remained on the wall, with a darker patch where her mother had once tried to clean it.

The clock settled crookedly. She stood on a chair and straightened it.

From there she could see the dust on top of the cupboards, a birthday candle, the lid of a jar.

She climbed down without touching them.

While the kettle boiled, she checked the clock against her phone. It was four minutes fast.

Her hand was already on the chair when she remembered her mother asking the time, then asking whether that was the real time or the kitchen time.

Helen left the chair where it was.

When the kettle clicked off, she could hear the clock."
